lead: This unit is about the two languages every browser understands: HTML5 for structure and CSS3 for presentation. You begin with a single file of tags and end with a responsive page layout built on Flexbox, Grid and Bootstrap. After it you can write, style and lay out a complete front-end page and read someone else's markup without guessing.
about: Unit 2 builds the visible half of a web application. Chapter 2.1 shows how an HTML document is structured: tags, elements, attributes and the tree the browser builds. Chapter 2.2 adds the everyday content pieces, namely text, links, lists, tables and images. Chapter 2.3 covers forms, the only way a page sends data back to a server. Chapter 2.4 replaces layout divs with HTML5 semantic elements and adds audio, video and iframes. Chapters 2.5 to 2.7 move to CSS: how rules are written and included, how the box model decides every width, and how colour, background and type are set. Chapter 2.8 makes pages responsive with positioning, Flexbox, Grid and media queries. Chapter 2.9 shows Bootstrap, which packs all of this into ready-made classes.

chapters.idea: An HTML document is a tree of nested elements, and every element is written with tags and tuned with attributes.
chapters.depth: Doctype, html, head, body, title, meta charset and viewport, link for stylesheets, script. The three words students mix up: a tag is the markup, an element is the whole start-tag plus content plus end-tag, an attribute is a name="value" pair inside the start tag. Void elements that never close (br, img, hr, input, meta, link), comments, case-insensitivity, global attributes id, class, style, title, lang. Show the tree in the browser's Elements panel. Some syllabi call this "basic tags and web navigation"; a few also mention XHTML rules (lowercase names, quoted attributes, self-closing tags).

figure.aria: The html element has two children: head, holding title, meta and link, and body, holding an h1 and a p that contains an em.

chapters.example: Write the smallest valid HTML5 page for a college notice board: a document title "Notices", a level-1 heading "Notices", one paragraph in which the word "today" is emphasised, and a link to an external stylesheet. Draw the element tree and count: html, head, title, meta, link, body, h1, p, em gives 9 elements; 7 are non-void and 2 (meta, link) are void.
chapters.trap: Confusing title (the browser tab) with h1 (the page heading), and closing a void element or nesting a p inside a p. The browser silently repairs both, so the page looks right while the tree is wrong.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: how a browser fetches a URL over HTTP and where the developer console lives.
chapters.leave: CSS rules and selectors (chapter 2.5); the JavaScript DOM API (Unit 3); pages generated on the server (Unit 4).

chapters.idea: A few content elements — headings, links, lists, tables and images — carry almost all the text and data a page shows.
chapters.depth: Inline formatting: b, strong, i, em, u, mark, small, sub, sup, code, pre, br, hr, headings h1 to h6. Hyperlinks: absolute vs relative URLs, href, target, mailto:, tel:, jump links to an id, an image inside a link. Lists: ul, ol with start and type, dl with dt/dd, nested lists. Tables: caption, thead, tbody, tfoot, th with scope, colspan, rowspan, never for layout. Images: src, required alt, width/height, loading, figure with figcaption. Deprecated presentational attributes (align, bgcolor) are named only to say CSS replaced them.

figure.title: Table grid: 3 columns, 4 rows, one colspan
figure.aria: Four table rows of three columns; in the last row the word Sum covers the first two columns because that cell has colspan 2, and 70 sits in the third column.

chapters.example: Build a price table with header row Item, Qty, Rs; body rows Pen 2 20 and Ink 1 50; and a footer row where one cell reading Sum has colspan="2" and the last cell reads 70. Show the 3-by-4 grid, mark which cells the footer cell covers, and check the arithmetic: 20 + 50 = 70.
chapters.trap: Swapping colspan (merge across columns) with rowspan (merge down rows), and using the old align or bgcolor attributes instead of CSS.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1: elements, attributes and correct nesting.
chapters.leave: Borders and table styling (chapters 2.6 and 2.7); file upload of images (Unit 4); building these nodes with JavaScript (Unit 3).

chapters.idea: A form turns typed input into name=value pairs and sends them to a server as a query string or a request body.
chapters.depth: The form element with action and method. Controls: input types text, password, email, number, tel, date, radio, checkbox, file, hidden, search, url, range, colour, submit, reset; textarea, select with option and optgroup, datalist, button. label linked by for/id, fieldset with legend. Attributes: name, value, placeholder, required, readonly, disabled, pattern, min, max, step, autocomplete, and the browser's built-in validation. GET puts pairs in the URL, POST puts them in the body; the server side is not covered here.

figure.aria: A form with action /search and method get holds a text input named q and a select named lang; pressing the submit button builds the URL /search?q=html&lang=en.

chapters.example: A search box has a text input with name="q" holding the value html, a select with name="lang" whose selected option has value en, and a submit button. The form uses action="/search" and method="get". Write the markup and the URL the browser requests after submission: /search?q=html&lang=en.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the name attribute: a control without a name is never sent, so the server receives nothing even though the user typed something. Radio buttons also need one shared name with different values to form a single-choice group.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.1 and 2.2 (attributes, nesting, labels as inline text); Unit 1 for URLs and HTTP methods.
chapters.leave: Reading GET and POST in PHP, cookies and sessions (Unit 4); validating with JavaScript (Unit 3); React controlled forms (Unit 5); posting with fetch or AJAX (Unit 3).

chapters.idea: HTML5 adds named regions that describe a page's structure and native tags that play media, so no plugin or div-soup is needed.
chapters.depth: Semantic elements header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure with figcaption, details with summary, time, mark, progress, meter; the rule that a section needs a heading, and article vs section. Multimedia: video and audio with src, controls, autoplay, muted, loop, preload, poster, several source children for different formats, track for captions. Frames: iframe with src, title, width, height, sandbox; frameset and marquee are obsolete and only named so students recognise old exam questions; a one-line mention of canvas and inline SVG.

figure.aria: Five semantic regions stacked in source order: header, nav, main, aside, footer.

chapters.example: Mark up a news page made of five blocks: a masthead with the site name, a menu of four links, one story with a heading and two paragraphs, a sidebar of three related links, and a copyright line. Name the semantic element for each block, give the nesting order, and say which are landmark regions. Then add a 90-second video with controls, a poster image and a caption track.
chapters.trap: Writing div class="header" where header is meant, and scattering section with no heading inside; the outline becomes meaningless. Old frame questions also expect you to say frameset is obsolete and iframe replaces it.
chapters.leave: Styling these regions with Flexbox and Grid (chapter 2.8); media element control through JavaScript (Unit 3); responsive images with srcset in depth (chapter 2.8).

chapters.idea: A CSS rule is a selector plus declarations, and when rules clash the cascade and specificity decide the winner.
chapters.depth: Rule anatomy: selector { property: value; }, comments, semicolons, units px, em, rem, %, vw and vh. Three ways to include styles: inline style attribute, internal style element in the head, external file through link rel="stylesheet"; @import and why it is slower. Selectors: universal *, type, class, id, attribute, grouping with a comma, descendant (space), child >, adjacent +, general sibling ~, pseudo-classes :hover, :focus, :first-child, :nth-child(2n), :not(), pseudo-elements ::before, ::after, ::first-line. The cascade, inheritance and the four-part specificity counter; !important. Some syllabi call this topic "CSS types".

figure.title: Specificity as four counters: inline, id, class, element
figure.aria: Five selectors with their four specificity counters; the id counter of #intro p is set, and the inline-style row wins on the first counter.

chapters.example: Two rules hit the same paragraph: #intro p { color: blue } and p.note { color: red }. Compare the counters (0,1,0,1) against (0,0,1,1): the id counter decides first, so the text is blue. Then add style="color: green" on the element and it becomes green with (1,0,0,0). Finally mark the red rule !important and it wins again.
chapters.trap: Adding the counters and calling equal values a tie (0+1+0+1 and 0+0+1+1 both give 2). Compare left to right, position by position, never by sum.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 (the link and style elements) and chapter 2.2 (inline elements to style).
chapters.leave: Preprocessors such as Sass (chapter 2.9 mentions them only); dynamic class changes with JavaScript (Unit 3); CSS-in-JS in React (Unit 5).

chapters.idea: Every element is a content box wrapped by padding, border and margin, and the four widths add up to the space it occupies.
chapters.depth: The four layers and what each one does. width and height size the content box by default; the total rendered width is content + left/right padding + left/right border, and margins push neighbours away without being part of the box. box-sizing: border-box and why designers set it globally. Shorthands: padding and margin with one, two, three or four values; border-width, border-style, border-colour and border shorthand with order; border-radius. margin: auto for centring, negative margins, vertical margin collapse between siblings and parent/child. display as block, inline and inline-block and how each treats width and vertical margins. overflow and outline vs border.

figure.aria: Four nested layers from outside in: a 10px transparent margin, a 5px solid border, 20px of padding, and the 300px content box.

chapters.example: A card is declared width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid black; margin: 10px. Find the rendered width: 300 + 20 + 20 + 5 + 5 = 350 px, and the space it blocks out with margins: 350 + 10 + 10 = 370 px. Then set box-sizing: border-box and find the new content width: 300 − 40 − 10 = 250 px.
chapters.trap: Assuming width: 300px gives a 300px box: padding and border sit outside it unless border-box is set. Vertical margins of two stacked blocks also collapse into the larger one, not the sum.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 for selectors and units; chapter 2.2 for the elements being boxed.
chapters.leave: Laying boxes side by side with Flexbox and Grid (chapter 2.8); Bootstrap's spacing utilities (chapter 2.9).

chapters.idea: Colour, background, font and text properties are ordinary CSS declarations, and each accepts several equivalent notations.
chapters.depth: Colour values: 140-odd keywords, #RRGGBB and #RGB shorthand, rgb() and rgba(), hsl() and hsla(), currentColor, opacity versus the alpha channel. Backgrounds: background-color, background-image, background-repeat, background-position, background-size with cover and contain, background-attachment, linear-gradient and radial-gradient, the shorthand order. Fonts: font-family with a fallback stack and generic families serif, sans-serif, monospace; @font-face and web fonts named without any URL; font-size, font-weight 100 to 900, font-style, line-height. Text: text-align, text-decoration, text-transform, letter-spacing, word-spacing, text-indent, text-shadow, white-space. The difference between em (parent size) and rem (root size).

figure.title: One colour in three notations
figure.aria: The same colour written three ways: hex FF 63 47, rgb 255 99 71, and hue 9, saturation 100 percent, lightness 64 percent.

chapters.example: A sale badge uses #FF6347. Write it as rgb() and as hsl(): FF = 255, 63 = 99, 47 = 71, so rgb(255, 99, 71). For hsl, max = 255 and min = 71 give lightness (255 + 71) ÷ 2 ÷ 255 ≈ 64%; the range is full so saturation is 100%; hue = 60 × (99 − 71) ÷ 184 ≈ 9°. So hsl(9, 100%, 64%). With 60% opacity it becomes rgba(255, 99, 71, 0.6).
chapters.trap: Treating hex pairs as decimal (FF is 255, not 15) and giving the alpha in rgba() as 0–255 instead of 0–1. Also, em multiplies by the parent font size while rem always multiplies by the root.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 (declarations and units) and chapter 2.6 (what padding, border and text live inside).
chapters.leave: Animated colour and hover transitions (chapter 2.8 mentions the transition property only); theme variables in Bootstrap and Sass (chapter 2.9).

chapters.idea: Positioning, Flexbox, Grid and media queries place boxes on the page and let one layout serve phone, tablet and laptop.
chapters.depth: Normal flow and display. Positioning: static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky, with top/right/bottom/left, the containing block rule, z-index and stacking order; floats and clear named as the old technique. Flexbox: display: flex, flex-direction, justify-content, align-items, align-self, flex-wrap, gap, flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, the flex shorthand and order. Grid: display: grid, grid-template-columns and rows, the fr unit, repeat(), minmax(), auto-fit and auto-fill, grid-template-areas, grid-column and grid-row span, gap. Responsive design: the viewport meta tag, mobile-first @media (min-width: 768px) queries, relative units, responsive images with max-width: 100%, srcset and picture.

figure.aria: A 600px flex container holds three items with flex values 1, 2 and 1, so their widths are 150, 300 and 150 pixels.

chapters.example: A flex container is 600 px wide with three items of flex: 1, flex: 2 and flex: 1 and no gap. Shares add to 4, so the widths are 600 × 1/4 = 150 px, 600 × 2/4 = 300 px and 150 px. Now add gap: 30px between items: free space is 600 − 60 = 540 px, so the widths become 135, 270 and 135 px.
chapters.trap: Using position: absolute and finding the element at the page corner, because it measures from the nearest ancestor with a position other than static. In Grid, a fixed fr track also overflows once an item carries a min-width or long unbroken word.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.6 (box model) and chapter 2.5 (selectors, media query syntax, units).
chapters.leave: Bootstrap's ready grid (chapter 2.9); React or Angular layout components (Unit 5); moving layout work to the server (Unit 6).

chapters.idea: A CSS framework like Bootstrap ships a 12-column grid, components and utility classes so a layout is assembled from class names instead of new CSS.
chapters.depth: What a framework supplies: reset, grid, components and utilities, as a CSS file plus a JavaScript bundle. Bootstrap structure: container and container-fluid, row, col-*, the 12-column rule, gutters, and the breakpoints sm 576, md 768, lg 992, xl 1200 px, with xxl 1400 px added in version 5. Components: navbar, card, button, form, alert, modal; utilities such as m-3, p-2, text-center, d-flex. Version 4 needs jQuery for its JavaScript components and uses ml/mr; version 5 drops jQuery, uses ms/me and adds xxl. Customising through Sass variables; loading from a CDN or local files (named, no URLs). Alternatives: Tailwind, Bulma, Foundation, Materialize. Only a few universities go deeper into Sass and task runners here; the npm side belongs to Unit 6.

figure.title: Bootstrap rows on a 960px container
figure.aria: Three Bootstrap rows; each cell is a column and its number is its span out of 12, so row A has three 4-wide columns, row B has 8 and 4, and row C has a single 12-wide column.

chapters.example: A container is 960 px wide. Row A has three col-md-4 columns: each width is 960 ÷ 12 × 4 = 320 px, total 960 px. Row B has col-md-8 and col-md-4: 640 px and 320 px. Row C has one col-12: 960 px. Say what happens if a row gets three col-md-6 instead — spans total 18, so the third column wraps to a new line.
chapters.trap: Putting a col-* directly inside a container with no row in between, which loses the gutter alignment; and expecting columns to shrink when their spans add past 12, when Bootstrap wraps them instead.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.5 to 2.8: selectors, the box model, colour and type, and the Flexbox engine the Bootstrap grid is built on.
chapters.leave: npm, module bundlers and task runners (Unit 6); Reactstrap and other React UI kits (Unit 5); customising with Sass variables in depth, which only a few universities teach.

links: attributes and nesting carry straight into links, tables and images
labels, inputs and buttons follow the same element and attribute rules
a form is placed inside the semantic regions of a page
semantic elements give the selectors something meaningful to style
selectors and units decide the boxes the box model measures
the box fixes where borders, backgrounds and text sit
colour and type properties ride on the layout that Flexbox and Grid build
Bootstrap's grid and utilities are Flexbox with class names
